_doc: HAND-AUTHORED, T-1234. The written ruling on every unasserted PERSON unit the matched-research table of T-1232 does not reach: the book-domain person units and the letter-list name suspicions. tools/research_spend_ledger.py reads this file at the point where it would otherwise leave a unit unresolved, so a ruling here can only close a unit nothing else has already closed and can never overturn an assertion, a later_only or a refusal the readings themselves carry. Every rule below is stated once and every unit carries its own note; the gate fails on a ruling whose unit does not exist, on a ruling that never fires, and on a rule with no statement. NOTHING HERE EDITS A RESIDENT, MINTS A PERSON OR MOVES A CONFIDENCE. A hand-off is not a spend: it names the open ticket whose field owns the finding, and that ticket closing turns this file red, which is the point. T-1598 ADDED A SECOND KIND OF UNIT TO THIS FILE: the 34 `building` place readings in the 1835 issues of the Chicago Democrat and the Chicago American. They are here rather than in a derived register because each one is a judgement about what the ground can receive from a particular notice, which is the shape T-1234 wrote this file for; a tool that derived them would be deriving the judgement. NOTHING HERE PLACES A BUILDING, MOVES A STRUCTURE OR INVENTS A COORDINATE — a reading that names a standing building the structure layer holds was handed to T-1600, which wrote the corroboration onto the record — and T-1600 then took the hand-off's own mechanism away by making data/structures/ a target surface, so nine of those ten now close as `asserted` off the record they were written onto and are gone from this file entirely. That is what a hand-off is supposed to end as. The tenth named a building the town has not built and waited on T-1603, which RULED it: the house stands on Dearborn Street and reaches no seat there, so it closes in the aggregate as building stock and data/exclusions.json carries the guard against building it. Every reading in this file is now closed against a stated rule and no rule here hands work to an open ticket. T-1599 CARRIED THAT SECOND KIND OF UNIT BACK BEFORE THE SCENE YEAR: the 88 `building` place readings in the 1833 and 1834 issues of the Chicago Democrat. They are the harder half of T-1589, because a pre-scene notice can be REFUTED by the calendar as well as unseated by the page — under the ladder ratified 2026-09-03 an earlier source no more promotes an 1835 fact than a later one does — and because eleven of them turned out to be spent already, on a layer this ledger does not index: the building stands in the committed town under its own record in data/structures/, raised or dated from the very notice the unit carries. Each of those eleven names its structure id so the claim can be checked in one grep. NOTHING HERE PLACES A BUILDING, MOVES A STRUCTURE OR INVENTS A COORDINATE: the 23 readings that DO reach the plat — a lot and a block, a named corner, an offset from a building the town holds — are handed to T-1624, which owns carrying each one forward to 1835-07-01 or refusing it in writing with the plat in front of it. T-1624 SPENT THE THIRD KIND OF UNIT AND TOOK ITS OWN HAND-OFF AWAY. T-1599 left 23 of the 1833-34 newspaper building readings `unresolved` under `the_earlier_building_placement_waits_on_the_plat`, because each gave a lot-and-block, a named corner or an offset from a standing building and each needed three decisions a register may not make: which lot of which block, whether the 1835 town already carries the building, and whether the corpus carries it forward at all. All three are now made, with `data/traces/thompson_block_numbering.json`, `data/reconstruction/1835_lot_ledger.json` and `data/structures/` in front of them, and the work is written up in `docs/RESEARCH/plat_level_building_placements_1833_34.md`. SEVEN SEAT ONTO A COMMITTED LOT — including G. Spring's 'LOT No. 7, in block No. 16, one lot east of Haddock's Tavern, on Lake street', the address that file was fetched for, which lands on `blk_south_water_dearborn#05`, south row, fronting Lake. NINE NAME A BLOCK THE LOT GRID DOES NOT REACH, one is on the school section and off this ground, and six anchor on another building and reach no lot. EVERY ONE OF THE TWENTY-THREE REFUSES THE FORWARD CARRY: the ladder ratified 2026-09-03 does not let an 1834 notice assert an 1835 fact, and the refusal is the finding. The hand-off rule is DELETED rather than left standing empty, which is what a spent hand-off is supposed to look like. Nothing here places a building, moves a structure, invents a coordinate or raises a confidence; the one placement question the plat work opened — whether these notices re-seat `mansion_house` on plat lot 6 of block 16 — is a structure move and a bake and is filed as T-1679. T-1625 DISCHARGED THE LAST HAND-OFF IN THIS FILE, and it is the first ruling here that carries an ASSERTION onto a structure and a household rather than only closing a unit. `the_prose_placement_waits_on_the_corner_pass` named six prose placements the books and Norris give by corner, cross street or named neighbour and waited on the ticket that owned them; that ticket is closed, so the rule is GONE from this file rather than renamed, which is what the never-fires gate is for. Five of the six are refused in writing with the plat in front of them and the sixth is not in this file at all, because it closed WITHOUT a ruling and that is the outcome a hand-off is supposed to reach: Moses and Kirkland name Richard J. Hamilton as the builder of a house on the Michigan Street block face this project already holds a record for, and say he lived in it nineteen years, which is a SPAN enclosing 1835-07-01. That identification moved `hh_hamilton_richard_j`'s `lives_at` off `cobweb_castle` and wrote an `occupants` block onto `watkins_school_house`, both at `inferred` and neither promoted — a compilation of 1895 corroborates and dates and does not raise a confidence. Nothing in this file asserts it — the written ruling for it was drafted and then DELETED, because `natural_disposition` reads the record itself and closed the unit `asserted` off the card, and this file may only close a unit nothing else has already closed. The reasoning behind the identification lives on the two records and in `docs/RESEARCH/prose_building_placements_1832_34.md`, which is where a reader should go for it.

earlier_evidence_adds_no_1835_fact.statement: The unit is dated before 1 July 1835 and its person content does not reach the scene date: the person is dead, departed or elsewhere by then, or the reading only repeats what the card already holds at least as well. Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source later than the scene date corroborates, enriches and dates and never promotes — and an EARLIER source does not promote either, because a man at Chicago in 1818 or 1827 is not thereby at Chicago in 1835. The reading stands as committed chronology; no card is edited and no person is minted.

later_than_the_scene_date.statement: The unit's person fact is dated after 1 July 1835, so under T-0513's ladder it may corroborate and date and may not assert an 1835 fact. It is written here rather than caught by rule because the ledger's year test reads the first year printed in describes_date: a death on 15 October 1835 reads as the year 1835 and is not later than it, and an 1843 entry that gives a birth year first reads as 1815.

pre_1830_settler_roster.statement: A row of Moses and Kirkland's table of actual settlers at Chicago PRIOR TO 1830, naming a person the residents layer holds no card for and on which the books crosswalk states no merge and no refusal. The table's own preamble bounds it before 1830 and the reading states it licenses nothing about 1835-07-01, so the row is withheld from the town and carried to the borderline roster (T-1159) as a name the research read and did not admit.

identity_refused_in_the_crosswalk.statement: The books crosswalk has already refused this row by name, under this domain's standing rule that a merge needs a rule naming both spellings verbatim and that a surname-only merge is always a refusal. The ledger now carries that refusal instead of reading the row as work nobody has looked at.

handed_to_the_family_pass.statement: The unit names kin — a wife, a marriage, a household member — of a head this town holds. WAS T-1170 UNTIL T-1313 CLOSED ON 2026-09-18: that ticket was split into T-1312, T-1313 and T-1314, and with the last of the three done the parent is spent work a unit cannot defer to. The three read the relatives named in the CARDS' own prose; these two are book claims that reading never saw, so they go to T-1320 with the seven kin enrichments in the same position. A marriage names a spouse and creates nobody; a marriage names a spouse and creates nobody, and no household member is minted here. THE HANDOFF MOVED FROM T-1320 TO T-1335 ON 2026-09-18. T-1320 was scoped to the BOOK corpus alone — its title is the ties whose relative is ALSO a held resident, and the book-corpus relatives who are nobody here — and the retarget off T-1170's split pointed ALL FOUR domains at it, which it never covered. Its pass (tools/spend_book_kin.py, PR #1464) did the book job and closed, and 168 units read as deferring to spent work: 147 church, 12 newspapers, 7 residents, and 2 book units its own pass left unruled. T-1335 is the family pass proper and owns all of them. A closed ticket cannot own unresolved units, so the line hands on to live work rather than reading as spent.

handed_to_the_dated_role_pass.statement: The unit's only person content is a dated office or trade. T-1145 replaced the one-occupation resident field with dated plural roles and is SPLIT and spent — T-1229 wrote the schema, T-1254 migrated the external evidence, T-1255 put the run on the card. THE HANDOFF NAMED T-1296 IN PROSE AND T-1299 IN THE FIELD, AND BOTH HAVE NOW CLOSED. The prose reference was wrong when it was written: T-1296 is the land-sale purchaser ruling and never owned this field; T-1299, which the field named, is the ticket that made the four generators over the singular field agree, and it landed on 2026-09-24 as #26. T-1299 DID ITS OWN JOB AND DID NOT SPEND THIS UNIT. Sherman's card now carries a dated sheriff office, 1833-12-03 to 1835-07-15, covering the scene date, and the 1835 field reads it instead of none_recorded — but that office is sourced to the 1833-1835 press under its own claim, and nothing in this repository cites bk_fer2_042. The book says a different thing from the press run: Fergus's bracketed annotation prints the man ELECTED in 1834 and again in 1836, two dates bracketing the scene year, where the press gives a bound of mentions. So the handoff moves to T-1543, which owns citing the book against the office the press established — as corroboration and dating, never as the thing that puts him in the 1835 town, and never by flattening an election into a term of service. A closed ticket cannot own an unresolved unit, so the line hands on to live work rather than reading as spent.

named_as_a_visitor_not_a_resident.statement: The source itself names the person as a visitor to the settlement who went home again. That is stronger than the standing rule that a transaction is never a residence, because the document states the man was not living here, and the reading's value is the negative.

suspicion_is_not_a_reading.statement: A row of data/research/residents/letter_list_reading_suspicions.json, whose own preamble says it 'is not evidence of anything': suspected_reading is a SUSPICION, it is graded nothing, no source states it, no record carries it, and nothing downstream may read it as a name. A worklist for a pass working the page images is ruled on as what it is; the household keeps the name the letter list actually prints, and the rows stay for the image pass to work.

merge_target_withdrawn_from_the_layer.statement: A row of Moses and Kirkland's table of actual settlers prior to 1830 whose landed crosswalk merge names a resident card THIS LAYER NO LONGER HOLDS, the card having been withdrawn by a later refusal rather than renamed or folded. There is no card for the row to be spent onto, and minting one from it would put back the resident the withdrawal removed — on pre-1830 evidence that under the ladder ratified 2026-09-03 cannot place anybody on 1835-07-01 by itself. The row is withheld from the town and carried to the borderline roster (T-1159) as a name the research read and did not admit, and the stale merge is left standing in the crosswalk because a merge is an identity statement inside the research layer and was not wrong when it was made.

the_reading_is_spent_on_the_yard_and_not.statement: The unit is a town reading the SCENE has already taken and the person ledger cannot take. This ledger indexes two target surfaces — the residents layer and, since T-1508, the business layer — and a reading spent on the yard, the terrain or the shore lands on neither, so it stands `unresolved` while being, in fact, finished work. That is the same answer a ground reading gets: it is true, it is in the window, it is committed chronology that the layer citing it names by claim id, and it attaches to no person and no firm. Spending it in aggregate records what it did rather than leaving it queued behind a ticket that has closed. Nothing here edits the record that cites it, raises a trade, or moves a tier.

the_notice_documents_building_stock_and_.statement: A to-let, for-rent or for-sale notice that names a store, a dwelling, a house or a stable standing in Chicago and gives nothing that reaches a seat: no street, or a street and no corner, number or neighbour on it. The BUILDING IS DOCUMENTED and the town's building stock is what it counts toward; no record in data/reconstruction/1835_address_book.json and no structure in data/structures/ can receive it, because nothing in the reading says which one it is. Choosing a frontage for it would be inventing a coordinate, which AGENTS.md rule 1 and rule 2 both forbid, so the unit is closed in the aggregate and the notice stands as committed evidence of vacant floor rather than as a placement.

the_building_is_not_standing_at_the_scen.statement: The source's own words put the building AFTER 1835-07-01: a meeting called to consider measures for building one, a corner stone to be laid, a board of directors consulting on means of obtaining premises. The reading is kept, and it is kept as a NEGATIVE — on the scene date the district has no school house, the square carries no reading room, the new meeting house is not yet begun — which is worth as much to a reconstruction as a positive and is the reason a refusal here is not a deletion. No structure may be raised on it and no seat may be reserved for it.

the_issue_is_printed_after_the_scene_dat.statement: The issue is dated after 1835-07-01 and the building content it carries is first documented there. Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source later than the scene date corroborates, enriches and dates, and never promotes: a store advertised to let on 29 July, a three-storey auction room rented on 1 August, eight thousand bricks wanted on 29 August do not establish that building on 1 July, and a hotel named only in an August reward notice is corroborated by it and not placed by it. The reading stands as committed chronology of the weeks after the scene and nothing in the 1835 model is moved on it.

the_named_public_house_is_documented_to_.statement:
THE TENTH OF T-1600'S TEN, RULED RATHER THAN WAITED ON (T-1603). The rule this replaces was a hand-off: a notice naming a standing building the structure layer does not hold, held unresolved behind the ticket that owned building the house or refusing it. It is ruled here, and the ground of the ruling is not the ground the hand-off expected.

WHAT THE HAND-OFF HAD. The meeting notice puts the town's Democrats in the Eagle Coffee House, Trowbridge's, on Monday 29 June 1835 — two days before the scene date — so the house stands and is in business. For where it stood the hand-off had one line, from the Abell advertisement three columns away in the same issue, and that line is shredded: page 3 of 1835-06-24 is a strict line-by-line interleave of two real columns, the advertisement survives as every other line of itself, and the line carrying the preposition is gone. The 24 June pass named four readings that fit the fragment — 'opposite the', 'a few doors from the', 'nearly opposite the', 'in the rear of the' — and refused to choose. So the hand-off recorded that 'the street is nearly there and the seat is not'.

THE STREET IS NOT NEARLY THERE. IT IS DOCUMENTED, BY THE SAME ADVERTISEMENT REPRINTED WHOLE. The Democrat of 5 August 1835 sets Abell's notice again over the same 24 June 1835 copy date, on page 4 column 3, in a column that is not interleaved, and the missing line is there: 'Office with [E]sq. Harmon in Dearborn stre[et], two doors south of the "Eagle Coffee House."' (chicago_democrat_1835_08_05#c020). It is a FIFTH reading, none of the four the June pass enumerated — which is the argument for why that pass was right to refuse to choose. A second firm says the street independently: Cooley and Hol[b]man, tailors, have 'taken a shop on Dearborn Street, nearly opposite the [E]agle Coffee House' (chicago_democrat_1835_08_05#c005, reprinted 1835_08_19#c006). Two firms, three printings, one street. THE EAGLE COFFEE HOUSE STANDS ON DEARBORN STREET, and that is documented, not inferred.

AND THE SEAT IS STILL NOT THERE, BECAUSE THE ANCHOR GRAPH IS A CLOSED LOOP. Every neighbour the corpus gives the Eagle is measured FROM the Eagle: Abell and Esq. Harmon two doors south of it, the tailors' shop nearly opposite it. Neither of those two addresses is itself seated — the register classes all four readings `street_only` for exactly this reason, and their own limit_reason says the anchor 'names nothing the committed town holds'. So the only fixed thing in the whole set is Dearborn Street, which runs the length of the original town, and nothing in the corpus reached says which block, which side, or how far along. Choosing one would invent a coordinate, which AGENTS.md rule 1 and rule 2 both forbid, and it would invent it for a PUBLIC HOUSE — a building whose position is a fact about the town's political geography, since this is the room the Democrats moved their meetings into between 6 and 24 June 1835.

SO THE DISPOSITION IS THE ONE THIS FILE ALREADY USES FOR A DOCUMENTED BUILDING WITH NO SEAT, and the difference from `the_notice_documents_building_stock_and_no_seat` is worth stating: that rule covers a notice giving no street or a street with no neighbour on it, and this reading gives a street AND two neighbours. It reaches no seat anyway, because the neighbours are unseated too. A building this well attested and still unplaceable is a different finding from a to-let notice, and it counts toward the town's building stock in the same way. No structure is raised on it and no seat is reserved for it; `data/exclusions.json` carries the guard under `eagle_coffee_house` so the next reader does not helpfully build it. Nothing here is a judgement that the house did not exist — it plainly did, it had a keeper, and the corpus can name the street it stood in.

the_earlier_notice_documents_a_building_.statement: THE PRE-SCENE-DATE TWIN OF `the_notice_documents_building_stock_and_no_seat`, AND TWO THINGS STAND BETWEEN IT AND A PLACEMENT RATHER THAN ONE. A notice printed in 1833 or 1834 names a building standing in Chicago — a store, a dwelling, a tavern stand, a shop, a school house, a room let for offices, the house a meeting is called at — and reaches no seat: it gives no street, or a street with no corner, number or neighbour on it, or an anchor whose own position the committed town does not hold. THE BUILDING IS DOCUMENTED and the town's building stock in the two years before the scene is what it counts toward. Choosing a frontage for it would invent a coordinate, which AGENTS.md rule 1 and rule 2 both forbid. AND THE DATE IS THE SECOND BAR: under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source later than the scene date corroborates and never promotes, and an EARLIER source does not promote either — a building advertised to let in March 1834 is a fact about March 1834, and nothing in these notices says the same building stood on 1835-07-01 or which of the town's roofs it became. So even a seat would not place it in the scene, and it has no seat. Where the anchor is a building the town DOES hold but the notice gives no offset from it, the ground is the one T-1603 stated for the Eagle Coffee House: an anchor graph that closes on itself reaches no seat, and 'near' is not an offset a lot can be read off. Nothing here places a building, moves a structure or invents a coordinate.

the_earlier_reading_carries_no_building_.statement: THE READING'S BUILDING CONTENT IS NOT A BUILDING. It is the town around one, and it is spendable on nothing smaller than the town: the editor's own count of eight hundred souls inside the corporate limits; his count of seven or eight raisings in one week and his notice that the mechanics were at work and others arranging to put buildings up; a count of 122 building lots for sale in the school section; a platted parcel offered for sale or lease with nothing standing on it, whose lot and block are a claim about the LAND market and not about the fabric; an auction of town lots in 'the most business part of the town'; a corporation ordinance whose stove-pipe clause specifies the whole town's roofline rather than any one roof; an institution named with no premises at all. Every one is true, dated, inside or before the window, and committed chronology the reconstruction reasons from — and not one attaches to a resident, a firm or a structure record, which is the only reason it stands unresolved. This ledger indexes two target surfaces, the residents layer and (since T-1508) the business layer, and a reading spent on the TOWN lands on neither; that is the same answer `the_reading_is_spent_on_the_yard_and_not_on_a_person_or_a_firm` gives a ground reading. Spending it in aggregate records what it did. Nothing here raises a roof, moves a parcel or promotes a confidence.

the_earlier_notice_is_spent_on_a_structu.statement: THE TOWN HAS ALREADY TAKEN THIS READING, ON THE LAYER THIS LEDGER CANNOT SEE. The building the notice names stands in the committed town under its own record in `data/structures/`, and that record's own `documented_range` is dated or worded from this notice or from a sister printing of it. So the reading is finished work and nothing further is owed on it — it reads unresolved only because the ledger indexes the residents layer and the business layer and this reading landed on the STRUCTURE layer, which is the same blind spot `the_reading_is_spent_on_the_yard_and_not_on_a_person_or_a_firm` was written for. EVERY RULING UNDER THIS RULE NAMES THE STRUCTURE ID, so the claim is checkable in one grep and this rule cannot be used to wave a reading through: if the named record does not cite the issue, the ruling is wrong and says so out loud. What this rule does NOT do is upgrade anything. It adds no source to a record, moves no position, and promotes no confidence — the structures' positions stay at the grade they already carry, `reconstructed` or `inferred` as the case may be, and a pre-scene notice is not evidence that would raise one.

the_earlier_building_stands_outside_the_.statement: THE BUILDING IS PLACED, AND IT IS PLACED OFF THIS PROJECT'S GROUND. The notice's own words put it outside the reconstruction: a good log house and stable on a pre-emption claim thirteen miles from Chicago; a steam saw mill on the west half of the south-west quarter of section 4, township 39 north, range 14 east, which is up the North Branch and outside the plat; a dwelling house levied on in township 40 north, which is a township north of the one the town stands in; a tavern whose dateline is Springfield's and not Chicago's. These are the strongest placements in the run and that is the point — the survey description is exactly what carries them out of scope. They are kept, and the reason they are worth keeping is stated on each: the log house and its two thousand rails are the only description in the corpus of what an ordinary improved Cook county claim consisted of, and a name a reader will meet again inside the town travels with its caveat. Nothing is corrected to bring a building inside the plat: a wrong township is recorded as printed, because amending one to make a house fall in town would be inventing the placement.

the_prose_reading_corroborates_a_structu.statement: THE PROSE TWIN OF `the_earlier_notice_is_spent_on_a_structure_the_town_already_holds`, AND IT CLAIMS ONE THING LESS. The building the reading describes stands in the committed town under its own record in `data/structures/`, and what the reading carries is that building's form, use, occupancy or construction date. It is a recollection in a book, a compiled history or a civic finding, not a notice on a page, so it reaches the structure layer and nothing on the two surfaces this ledger indexes: not a resident, not a firm. THE ONE THING IT DOES NOT CLAIM is that the record was written from it. Most of these records were not: `grep` the structure id and the record's own sources and this page is usually absent, which is exactly why the rule says corroborates and not spent. AND THE RULE ADDS NOTHING. It writes no source onto a record, moves no position, and raises no confidence -- under the ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a recollection set down in 1881, 1884, 1895 or 1911 about a building of 1818 or 1833 may corroborate and may not promote, and a record's `documented` grade is not reachable from a page that is neither the source it stands on nor contemporary with the fact. Offering the corroboration to the record is the structures layer's own PR and its own judgement. EVERY RULING UNDER THIS RULE NAMES THE STRUCTURE ID, so the claim is checkable in one grep; where the reading disagrees with the record the ruling says so and resolves nothing, because an agreement manufactured between a plan and a pace-estimate is not evidence.

the_prose_reading_is_spent_on_the_scene_.statement: THE READING IS FINISHED WORK, AND THE WORK IT FINISHED WAS LEAVING A BUILDING OUT. `data/sidecars/1835/exclusions.json` is the scene's written list of structures this project researched and deliberately did not build, each with the evidence that dates it out; a reading that describes one of those buildings has already been spent, on the only decision it could ever have supported. Two shapes qualify and both name their id: the reading describes a building on the `excluded` list, or the reading is itself cited in the dossier under `docs/RESEARCH/` that put the building on that list. THE FIRST FORT AND THE OLD KINZIE MANSION ARE THE BULK OF IT -- `fort_dearborn_first_1803` burned in 1812 and the scene stands beside the 1816 rebuild; `kinzie_house` was last seen years before the window and no source attests its survival -- and a recollection of either is a recollection of a building that is not in this town. Nothing is drawn, moved or added, and no exclusion is reopened here: an exclusion is a ruling on the scene and this ledger does not overturn one from the research side.

the_prose_reading_carries_no_building_on.statement: THE PROSE TWIN OF `the_earlier_reading_carries_no_building_only_the_town_around_it`. The unit is filed `kind: building` and its building content is not a building: a garrison strength in companies, a parish register's opening date with no chapel, house or street in it anywhere on the page. It is true, dated and committed chronology the reconstruction reasons from, and it attaches to no resident, no firm and no structure record, which is the only reason it stood unresolved. It is spendable on nothing smaller than the town.

the_prose_building_stands_outside_the_re.statement: THE PROSE TWIN OF `the_earlier_building_stands_outside_the_reconstruction_ground`. The reading places its building, and the place is off this project's ground -- up the South Branch, out on the prairie, in another township. The placement is the strongest thing in the reading and that is precisely what carries it out of scope. It is kept for what it is good for, and nothing is bent to bring it inside the plat.

the_later_printed_reading_corroborates_t.statement: THE SOURCE IS PRINTED AFTER THE SCENE AND ITS BUILDING CONTENT SPANS THE SCENE DATE. That is the one shape in which a later page speaks to 1 July 1835 without being an 1835 source: not a fact dated after the window and carried back, but a span -- occupied, standing, in use from a year before to a year after -- inside which the scene date falls. Under the ladder ratified 2026-09-03 that corroborates and dates and does not promote: it cannot raise a confidence, it cannot place anything, and it is written here rather than left to the automatic rule because the automatic rule reads a describes_date and a span is not a date.

the_plat_placement_is_seated_and_the_for.statement: THE PLAT WORK IS DONE AND THE ANSWER IS A REFUSAL. The reading gives a lot number and a block number of the Original Town and both now resolve. `data/traces/thompson_block_numbering.json` carries Wright's numeral for all fifty-eight blocks, twenty-one of them stamped onto a committed block id, and its `lot_numbering` scheme — lots 4 3 2 1 across the north row west to east, 5 6 7 8 across the south row west to east, read on four blocks — puts the lot on a named cell of `data/reconstruction/1835_lot_ledger.json`. The seat is written down in `docs/RESEARCH/plat_level_building_placements_1833_34.md` so that nobody reads it a fourth time. WHAT THE SEAT DOES NOT BUY IS THE BUILDING. Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 an EARLIER source no more promotes an 1835 fact than a later one does, and a for-sale, auction or lien notice of 1833-34 says a building stood on that lot on the day the notice ran — twelve to twenty months before 1835-07-01 — and says nothing whatever about the scene date. So nothing is placed, no structure moves, no coordinate is invented and no confidence is raised: the placement is recorded as reasoning and the forward-carry is refused. Where the committed town already stands a roof on the same cell, it stands there from the policy deal of T-1199 and not from this notice, and the note below says so.

the_plat_placement_names_a_block_the_lot.statement: THE BLOCK IS READ AND THERE IS NO LOT TO SEAT IT ON. `data/traces/thompson_block_numbering.json` carries the numeral for all fifty-eight Original Town blocks, and only twenty-one of them are stamped onto a grid cell: `tools/generate_plat_lots.py` emits the three South Division tiers and nothing else, so the North Division's Kinzie-to-the-river tier, the West Division's eighteen and the Washington-Madison seven are held in that file's `blocks_not_in_the_grid` for exactly this reason — there is no id to stamp them onto. The lot number is worse placed still. The `lot_numbering` scheme is graded `conjectural`, it is read on four EIGHT-lot South Division blocks, and the same file records in `ten_lot_blocks` that the West Division's blocks carry TEN lots in two columns of five with the alley running north-south — a shape the scheme does not describe at all. So a lot number on one of these blocks cannot be carried to a committed cell without inventing the cell, and this project does not invent one. The forward-carry is refused on top of that, for the reason rule `the_plat_placement_is_seated_and_the_forward_carry_refused` states in full: an 1833-34 notice does not put a building on the ground on 1835-07-01. The block reading stands as committed chronology and the note below says which block was read and what is missing under it.

the_plat_placement_stands_on_the_school_.statement: THE BLOCK NUMBER IS NOT A TOWN-OF-CHICAGO BLOCK NUMBER. Thompson's plat numbers fifty-eight blocks and stops there; a three-figure block belongs to the canal and school-section subdivisions beyond it, and this project's own land-sale ground register names this one outright — “block 111 of the school section, section 16 T39N R14E” (`data/research/land_sales/ground.json`, and the same ground in `data/reconstruction/1835_land_sales_by_tract.json`). Section 16 lies south and west of Madison Street, outside the Original Town and outside the ground this reconstruction models or means to model. So the reading places its buildings off this project's ground in the same way the log house thirteen miles out and the steam saw mill in section 4 do. Nothing is seated, nothing is asserted against the buildings themselves, and the reading stands as committed evidence about a subdivision the scene does not reach.

the_offset_placement_reaches_no_committe.statement: THE READING PLACES ITS BUILDING AGAINST ANOTHER BUILDING, AND THE ANCHOR IS WHAT FAILS. These are the 1833-34 notices that give no lot and no block but an offset — in the rear of, next door to, nearly opposite — from a building somebody in 1834 could see from the street. With the plat and the structure layer in front of them, every one of these offsets ends in one of three ways and not one of them reaches a committed lot. EITHER the anchor is a building this project has deliberately not modelled: the post office after its move of about July 1834, which `data/structures/hogan_store.json` states in terms would be “almost entirely invention today”. OR the anchor stands in the committed town somewhere the notice does not put it, so accepting the offset would mean moving a placed record on the strength of a source earlier than the scene, which the ladder ratified 2026-09-03 does not license. OR the offset names a direction and no distance, and “opposite” across a corner reaches two blocks and four lots. The forward-carry is refused for the same reason it is refused everywhere in this set, and the anchor's disagreement is recorded rather than resolved — where it is worth its own work the note below names the ticket that owns it.

the_prose_placement_reaches_a_block_face.statement: THE PROSE TWIN OF `the_plat_placement_is_seated_and_the_forward_carry_refused`, AND IT REACHES ONE STEP LESS FAR. The reading gives a street and a cross street, or a corner, or a block number, and the plat work is now done: the street resolves on the committed grid and the ruling below names the block or blocks the locator reaches. What it never reaches is a LOT, because a cross street is not a lot number and 'near Franklin' is two blocks wide, and on the north bank Kinzie's Addition has no lot subdivision at all. WHAT THE FACE DOES NOT BUY IS THE BUILDING, for exactly the reason the plat-level rule gives: under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 an EARLIER source no more promotes an 1835 fact than a later one does, and a book's sentence about a building standing in 1832, or in use in 1834, says nothing whatever about 1 July 1835. So nothing is placed, no structure moves, no coordinate is invented and no confidence is raised: the block work is recorded as reasoning in `docs/RESEARCH/prose_building_placements_1832_34.md` so nobody reads it a third time, and the forward carry is refused. WHERE THE BUILDING IS A GAP THE TOWN OUGHT TO FILL the ruling says so and names the ticket that owns building it — which is a placement job on the reconstruction programme's own terms and not a carry from this page.

the_prose_offset_placement_has_no_commit.statement: THE READING PLACES ITS BUILDING AGAINST ANOTHER BUILDING AND THE ANCHOR IS NOT IN THE TOWN. The prose counterpart of `the_offset_placement_reaches_no_committed_lot`, and it fails one step earlier: those notices had anchors a reader could argue about, and these have none. An offset — 'near Mr. Noble's house', 'about 80 rods to the south of that' — is a measurement from a point, and the point has to be committed before the measurement means anything. Here the anchor is either a building this project holds no record for and has not excluded, so there is no coordinate to offset from and inventing one would be inventing the anchor as well as the building; or it is a building on `data/exclusions.json`, which is the project's written finding that it does not stand in this scene — and offsetting from a building the scene does not contain would place a second building on the authority of the first one's absence. Either way nothing is placed and no coordinate is derived. The forward carry is refused as well and separately: both readings in this shape describe 1832, and the ruling below says so rather than letting the anchor failure do two jobs.

the_prose_placement_is_undated_and_its_o.statement: THE LOCATOR IS THE BEST IN THE SET AND THE DATE IS MISSING, AND THE TWO HALVES ARE RULED SEPARATELY. A named corner of two committed streets is the strongest thing prose can give this project — stronger than a block, stronger than a cross street — and the ruling below resolves it on the grid so the work is not lost. Then it refuses, because the page gives the building no date at all: its own narrative brackets the event between a paragraph dated before the scene and a building put up after it, and 1835-07-01 lies inside that bracket. A locator cannot supply a date and a bracket is not one. THE PROJECT DOES NOT SPLIT A BRACKET, and the reason is stated on the ladder: choosing the half of an interval that puts a building in the scene is choosing the answer, and a run that does it once has no ground to refuse the next reading that wants the same favour. The candidate is recorded with the corner resolved and the bracket stated, so a second source that dates it lands on finished work; nothing is placed meanwhile. A NAME THE BUILDING GOT LATER IS NOT EVIDENCE EITHER WAY — where the reading knows the building by a name coined after the scene, the ruling says the name is anachronistic and does not treat that as dating the fabric.

rulings.note: Hubbard remembers John Crafts dying at Chicago of bilious fever in December, 'I think', of 1823; the old-settler death notice fdn0137 prints 1825. The crosswalk's merge leaves the two years unreconciled and this ruling does not pick one, because either way the man was a decade dead before 1 July 1835.

The silversmith trade and the agency here belong to John Kinzie the ELDER, who died in 1828, and the crosswalk refuses him onto the card of John Harris Kinzie, his son, which is the town's. An occupation of about 1822-23 for a man this layer does not model.

An undated Michilimackinac outfit among entries of 1822, sending Jean Bt. Beaubien to trade at MILWAUKEE. His card already carries 'Detroit and the Milwaukee trade' as an attested origin off Andreas, so the entry corroborates thirteen years early and adds nothing.

An outfit of 22 August 1821 to William H. Wallace, with Hurlbut's own hedge that he was 'understood to have died in Chicago about 1826'. The residents layer holds no William H. Wallace and this reading mints none.
Oseemit speaking at Fort Wayne in 1811, twenty-four years before the scene date, and about the range of the Potawatomi rather than about any person at Chicago in 1835.

Beckwith names Billy Caldwell's wife as the sister of Min-ne-mung, the Yellow Head. Caldwell is a head this town holds and the crosswalk merges the naming; the kin tie itself is a family fact and belongs to the pass that gives the attested heads the families the sources name.

Silas Wooster Sherman, whom this layer holds as Silas W Sherman, annotated as elected sheriff of Cook County in 1834 and again in 1836. A dated civic office across the scene year is exactly the dated-role field, and it may not be flattened into the single occupation the record carries today.

Robert Fergus's own directory entry gives his arrival at Chicago as 1 July 1839, four years after the scene date. The ledger's year test reads 1815, the first year printed in describes_date, and cannot see the arrival.
The obituary dates Thomas J. V. Owen's death to 15 October 1835, three and a half months after the scene date. It bears on a scene set later in the year and asserts nothing about 1 July.
A Dr Spring died on 10 November 1835. The line gives no given name, so it cannot be tied to the G. Spring of T-0423 even as a death; it is later than the scene date on top of that.
The Rev. Jesse Walker died twelve miles west of Chicago on 5 October 1835, three months after the scene date.
Hollis Newton, hotel-keeper, died on 25 August 1835, seven weeks after the scene date, and the list gives no house and no street.
The Rev. Allen B. Freeman died on 17 December 1834, aged 27, six months before the scene date; the town of 1 July 1835 does not hold him and this reading does not put him in it.
Dr Alexander Wolcott, the Indian agent, died on 25 October 1830. Wolcott Street carries his name in this project's street list and that is the whole of what survives him here.

John Kinzie the elder, entered as settling in 1803 and dead on 6 January 1828. The volume's 'first white American settler' is a claim held at arm's length and graded tier 3; neither half reaches 1835.

Hubbard meets John H. Kinzie at Mackinaw in 1818 and is explicit that he was stationed permanently there. The crosswalk's merge says in terms that it does not follow he was at Chicago in 1818, and 1818 is not 1835 either way.

The elder John Kinzie residing at Chicago in 1818, in the words of a man carrying a letter of introduction to the house. Seventeen years early, and about the father rather than the son this town holds.

Five members of the elder Kinzie's household met at his table in 1818. The crosswalk's own merge of Robert Kinzie says it does not follow that he is placed anywhere in 1835 by this source, and the same is true of the other four.

The fort's commanders from 3 October 1828, and the list STOPS at 19 June 1833 because Hubbard could not find the later names in the War Department records. It therefore names nobody commanding Fort Dearborn in 1835 and is recorded as a limit.

The Kinzies and Dr Wolcott rendering Hubbard kind services on his arrival in the autumn of 1822 or 1823; the page does not print the year and this reading does not invent one. Thirteen years before the scene.
Pierre Chouteau, Jr. of St Louis at Chicago for a fortnight in 1822 or 1823. A stay of two weeks is what the reading says it is; no residence at Chicago follows for him in that year or in 1835.
The Indian trader's place at Chicago changing hands in 1827-28, Hubbard applying and not receiving it. A lead on the town's offices seven years before the scene and no person fact of 1835.

Shaub-e-nee a guest of Billy Caldwell at Chicago on the evening before Cass's visit of July 1827. The crosswalk's merge of Caldwell states that it does not follow he is placed at Chicago in 1835, and Shaub-e-nee is not a resident of this town at all.

St. Cyr permitted to remain at Chicago, having been sent by Bishop Rosati in 1833. The crosswalk's merge says his record is not edited: the arrival is already graded attested at year precision off Andreas, so a 1921 digest repeating it adds nothing the card does not hold at least as well.

John Dean Caton married Laura Adelaide, daughter of Jacob Sherrill, in 1835 — the year only. The scene date sits inside it and the sentence cannot say which side, so the marriage is a family fact for the pass that draws spouses and not an 1835 household of two.

The Rev. Allen B. Freeman and his wife Hannah C. arrived at Chicago on 16 August 1833 — an arrival to the day, for a man the same volume says died of typhoid in December 1834. Neither of them is in the town of 1 July 1835 and no arrival is carried onto a card that does not exist.

Charles Butler and Arthur Bronson are named by the town's own historians as VISITORS to the settlement from New York who went home again and sent books back. The passage is evidence against a residence, which is what T-1017 turned on, and it is recorded as the negative it is.
Ament, Edward G — no nativity cell and one undated civic act. The residents layer holds no Ament at all.
Anderson, Joseph against Eli F Anderson, the only Anderson this layer holds; the forenames are different words and a surname-only merge is always a refusal in this domain.

Caldwell, Archibald against Billy Caldwell (Sauganash), the only Caldwell this layer holds and a man merged in this same pass from a different row of this same table. The remarks cell's '1st tavern 1829' licenses nothing about a tavern standing on 1835-07-01.

Crafts, John — the layer holds no Crafts, and this is the trader whom bk_afc_010 and the old-settler notice put dead at Chicago in 1823 or 1825.
Galloway, James — a name, a state, a year and one civic act, and no Galloway in the residents layer.

Jouett, Charles — first Indian agent, the remarks cell reading 'left in 1881' where the digits are one transposition from 1811 and Jouett's agency ended that year. An office of 1805-11 and no card in the layer.
Kinzie, John — the row's own remarks cell ends 'died 1828', which is John Kinzie the ELDER. He belongs in no 1835 record at all and the crosswalk refuses him onto his son's card.

Ouilmette, Antoine — the layer holds no Ouilmette. On the nativity cell, see the Laframboise rows: it is the compiler's classification and not a birthplace.
